byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: A nation of 179 million, seven in ten in towns and cities, with nearly 74 million motor vehicles and a baby boom still under way.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1960 census counted 179.3 million people, 50.6 to the square mile.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: Decennial census historical facts, 1960
World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A baby born in 1960 could expect to live nearly 70 years.

items.title: Town and city
items.summary: About 70 percent of Americans lived in urban areas.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Urban population (% of total)

items.title: Infant deaths
items.summary: About 26 of every 1,000 babies died before their first birthday.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)

items.title: Births per woman
items.summary: The fertility rate was 3.65 births per woman, near the peak of the baby boom.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Fertility rate, total (births per woman)

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations reached 73.9 million: 61.7 million cars, 11.9 million trucks and 272,000 buses.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: A frozen dinner in an aluminium tray was a new way to put supper on the table, and a pizza chain opened its first shop.

items.title: The first Domino's
items.summary: The first Domino's Pizza opened in Ypsilanti, Michigan, on 9 December 1960.

items.title: A tray with dessert
items.summary: In 1960 Swanson added desserts such as apple cobbler and brownies to a new four-compartment tray, and Banquet and Morton also began selling frozen dinners.

foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 grocery prices, appliance counts or typical meals.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Women wore knee-length shift dresses, pillbox hats and bouffant hair; men wore slim, single-breasted suits with narrow ties.

items.title: The shift dress
items.summary: Simple knee-length shift dresses were in style, while André Courrèges began experimenting with hemlines in the early 1960s.

items.title: The pillbox hat
items.summary: The pillbox hat was popularised largely through Jacqueline Kennedy, who favoured tailored suits and long gloves.

items.title: Bouffant and beehive
items.summary: Bouffant hair dominated, with beehives early in the decade, and pumps with lower heels and squared toes were the usual shoe.

items.title: Slim continental suits
items.summary: By 1962 slim, single-breasted continental suits and skinny ties, often in grey flannel, mohair or sharkskin, were fashionable in the United States and Britain; Pierre Cardin showed collarless suits in 1960.

items.title: Plaid shirts and blue jeans
items.summary: Teens and casual wearers favoured plaid button-down shirts with slim blue jeans, and capri pants and stretch ski pants appeared.

items.title: Wrinkle-free fabrics
items.summary: Nylon, orlon and terylene were promoted as cheap and wrinkle-free.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A production worker in manufacturing earned about $90 a week.

items.title: A manufacturing paycheque
items.summary: A production worker in manufacturing earned $2.26 an hour, or $89.72 a week, on average; in durable goods $97.44 and in non-durable goods $80.36.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4361-4366: Hourly and weekly earnings of production workers in manufacturing, 1909-1995

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures for 1960 working hours, women's work or the minimum wage.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: The school year was 178 days, and in November six-year-old Ruby Bridges began walking into a school that had been closed to her.

items.title: The school year
items.summary: The average school term was 178.0 days, a pupil attended 160.2 of them, and 90 percent of enrolled pupils were present on a given day.

sources.label: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2003, Table 36: school term and attendance, 1869-70 to 1999-2000

items.title: Desegregating the first grade
items.summary: On 14 November 1960 Ruby Bridges and the three girls known as the McDonogh Three became the first Black children to attend an all-white elementary school in Louisiana.

sensitivity.note: This item concerns racial segregation and the hostility children faced.

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures on 1960 enrolment, school costs or toys.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: In December the Supreme Court ruled segregation in interstate bus terminals illegal.

items.title: Boynton v. Virginia
items.summary: On 5 December 1960 the Supreme Court ruled in Boynton v. Virginia that segregation in public transit was illegal.

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 fares, journey times or air travel figures; the vehicle count is under The year in numbers.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 postage, telephone or television figures.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: The first birth-control pill was approved in May.

items.title: The pill is approved
items.summary: On 9 May 1960 the FDA announced approval of Searle's Enovid for contraception, the first oral contraceptive pill.

healthAndMedicine.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 doctor fees, hospital costs or vaccination figures.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: Evenings were for television, and for the debate that put two candidates in living rooms.

items.title: The first televised debate
items.summary: Richard Nixon and John F. Kennedy held the first televised presidential debate on 26 September 1960.

items.title: The Flintstones
items.summary: The Flintstones aired its first episode on ABC on 30 September 1960.

items.title: The annual Wizard of Oz
items.summary: CBS reran The Wizard of Oz on 11 December 1960, a year after its previous telecast, starting the tradition of annual showings.

items.title: A trip to see Psycho
items.summary: Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho was released on 16 June 1960 and Ben-Hur won eleven Academy Awards that April.

items.title: A walk-off in the World Series
items.summary: The Pittsburgh Pirates beat the New York Yankees in Game 7 of the World Series on 13 October 1960 on Bill Mazeroski's home run.

spotlight.title: Suburbs, TV dinners and the family car
spotlight.standfirst: Americans were eating supper from foil trays in front of the television, driving 74 million vehicles, and leaving the big cities' centres.

items.title: The TV dinner
items.summary: Swanson's TV dinner, developed in 1953 and first sold for 98 cents, was a turkey, cornbread-stuffing, peas and sweet-potato meal with each food in its own compartment.

items.title: Big cities lose people
items.summary: Between the 1960 and 1970 censuses Detroit fell from 1,670,144 to 1,511,482, Cleveland from 876,050 to 750,903, Chicago from 3,550,404 to 3,366,957 and New York from 8,175,133 to 7,894,862.
